classification.difficultyReason: Compare gradients to explain why two apparent triangles enclose different areas.

inlines.text: Four identical pieces can be rearranged to give the two figures shown below. These figures are apparently identical
triangles, except that the second figure has a
Where did the missing square go? Hint: We noted that each of the figures is
a triangle. Test this claim by finding the gradients of the slanted sides of the orange and red pieces.

spec.description: Upper arrangement of four identifiable pieces on a unit grid. The red and orange slanted edges meet at (8,3).
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and piece boundaries are visible.

spec.description: Lower arrangement of the same four pieces on a unit grid, retaining the unfilled unit square between x=7 and x=8 on the baseline.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens, piece boundaries and the original hole are visible.

answer.short:
Orange gradient $=\frac25$; red gradient $=\frac38$.

The slanted edges have different gradients, so neither figure is a triangle. Their bent boundaries account for the unit-square difference in enclosed area.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}m_{\text{orange}}&=\frac25\\m_{\text{red}}&=\frac38\end{align*}$$
Since $\frac25\ne\frac38$, the two slanted edges do not form one straight line. The upper boundary bends inwards and the lower boundary bends outwards. The lower outline encloses one square unit more area, which appears as the hole; no piece is missing.
